questions.prompt: For a transfer function \(H=N(s)/D(s)\), what are the 'poles' and 'zeros'?
options: Poles are the roots of the numerator; zeros are the roots of the denominator
Poles are the frequencies where \(H=0\); zeros are the frequencies where \(|H|=1\)
Zeros are the roots of the numerator N (where \(H=0\)); poles are the roots of the denominator D (where H blows up)
Poles and zeros are both roots of the denominator, for the real and imaginary parts respectively
questions.explanation:
Zeros ('stakes in the ground' of the tent) are values of s where the numerator vanishes, so \(H=0\). Poles are values of s where the denominator vanishes, so \(|H|\to\infty\) (the poles holding the tent up) (reader Sec. 2.3.2).
The other options swap the roles or invent definitions.

questions.prompt: The RC low-pass filter has \(H(s)=1/(1+s\tau)\). Where is its pole?
options: At \(s=+1/\tau\)
At \(s=-1/\tau\) (on the negative real axis)
At \(s=j\tau\)
questions.explanation:
Set the denominator to zero: \(1+s\tau=0\) ⇒ \(s=-1/\tau\). A negative real pole means a decaying exponential \(e^{-t/\tau}\) in the response. The magnitude of the pole, \(1/\tau\), is the corner (break) frequency in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
A positive pole would mean an exponentially growing response (unstable); \(s=0\) would be an integrator.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass has \(R=1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) and \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\). At what angular frequency \((\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s})\) is its pole?
questions.explanation:
\(H(s)=1/(1+sRC)\) has its pole at \(s=-1/(RC)=-1/(10^{3}\times 10^{-6})=-1000\). The pole frequency is \(\omega_{p}=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\ (f_{p}=159\ \mathrm{Hz})\).
Common mistake: answering in Hz (159 Hz) when asked for \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).

questions.prompt: The transfer function \(H(s)=(s+200)/(s^{2}+30s+200)\) has real poles. What is the magnitude, in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), of the pole CLOSEST to the origin (the lowest-frequency pole)?
questions.explanation:
Factor the denominator: \(s^{2}+30s+200=(s+10)(s+20)\), so the poles are at \(s=-10\) and \(s=-20\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). The zero (from \(s+200=0\)) is at \(s=-200\).
The pole closest to the origin has magnitude \(10\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Common mistake: reading −200 (the zero) as a pole, or using the sum 30.

questions.prompt: An RC high-pass filter has \(H(j\omega)=j\omega\tau/(1+j\omega\tau)\), \(\tau=1\ \mathrm{ms}\). Which statement describes its pole and zero?
options: One zero at \(s=0\) and one pole at \(s=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
One zero at \(s=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and one pole at \(s=0\)
One zero at \(s=0\) and one pole at \(s=+1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
No zero, and one pole at \(s=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
questions.explanation:
With \(s=j\omega\): \(H(s)=s\tau/(1+s\tau)\). The numerator vanishes at \(s=0\) (a zero at the origin: no DC transmission). The denominator vanishes at \(s=-1/\tau=-1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (a pole in the left half-plane).
• Swapping the two reverses the high-pass into something like an integrator.
• A positive pole would mean an unstable (growing) response.
• The numerator is not a constant, so there is a zero.

questions.prompt: A circuit has \(H(s)=1000(s+400)/((s+20)(s+2000))\). What is its DC gain \(H(0)\)?
questions.explanation:
At DC, \(s=0\): \(H(0)=1000\times 400/(20\times 2000)=400{,}000/40{,}000=10\).
In normalized form, \(H=10(1+s/400)/[(1+s/20)(1+s/2000)]\): DC gain 10, a zero at \(400\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), poles at 20 and \(2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Common mistake: including s in the DC evaluation or forgetting the factor 1000.

questions.prompt: A circuit contains two capacitors and three resistors (and a voltage source). Which statement about the number of poles of its transfer function is correct?
options: There are always exactly 2 poles
There are 5 poles, one for each element
There are no poles unless an inductor is present
There are at most 2 poles, and fewer if the capacitors are not independent (e.g., two capacitors in parallel behave as one)
questions.explanation:
The number of poles equals the number of independent energy-storage elements (the order of the circuit's differential equation) (reader Sec. 2.3.2). Resistors do not add poles.
Two capacitors in parallel combine into \(C_{1}+C_{2}\) (one independent state) and give only one pole; so can a capacitor loop or a capacitor in series with another one, depending on the connection. So 'at most 2', not always 2.
RC circuits have poles without any inductor.

questions.prompt: A circuit has \(H(s)=(s+500)/(s^{2}+1500s+500000)\). Which description of its behavior is correct?
options: It is second-order with poles at 500 and \(1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), plus a zero at \(500\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) that makes it a high-pass
It has a single pole at \(500\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
The zero at −500 cancels the pole at −500, so it behaves like a single-pole low-pass with a pole at \(1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)
It has two complex poles and shows resonant peaking
questions.explanation:
Factor the denominator: \(s^{2}+1500s+500000=(s+500)(s+1000)\). So \(H=(s+500)/[(s+500)(s+1000)]=1/(s+1000)\).
The zero at −500 cancels one pole exactly, leaving a first-order low-pass with pole at \(1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\ (DC\) gain \(10^{-3}\)).
• Don't count the cancelled pair as separate features.
• The remaining pole is at 1000, not 500.
• The discriminant \(1500^{2}-4(500000)=250{,}000>0\), so the poles are real (no peaking).

questions.prompt: A series RLC circuit with \(R=50\ \Omega\), \(L=10\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(C=25\ \mu\mathrm{F}\) has output across C: \(H(s)=1/(1+sRC+s^{2}LC)\). Its poles are real. What is the magnitude, in \(\mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), of the HIGHER-frequency pole?
questions.explanation:
Poles satisfy \(s^{2}LC+sRC+1=0\), i.e., \(s^{2}+(R/L)s+1/(LC)=0\), with \(R/L=5000\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) and \(1/(LC)=4\times 10^{6}\ s^{-2}\).
\(s=[-5000\pm\sqrt{5000^{2}-4\times 4\times 10^{6}}]/2=[-5000\pm\sqrt{9\times 10^{6}}]/2=(-5000\pm 3000)/2\to s=-1000\) and \(-4000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\).
The higher pole has magnitude \(4000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Notice neither pole equals \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}=2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) or \(R/L=5000\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\): the poles split around \(\omega_{0}\) (their geometric mean is \(\omega_{0}\): \(\sqrt{1000\times 4000}=2000\)).
Common mistake: using \(\omega_{0}=2000\) for both poles.

questions.prompt: Preview of Bode plots. A later skill says: each pole bends the magnitude slope by \(-20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) at its break frequency, and each zero bends it by \(+20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\). For \(H(s)=1000(s+400)/((s+20)(s+2000))\), what is the slope of |H| (in \(\mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\)) between \(400\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) and \(2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\)?
options: \(-20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\)
\(0\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\) (flat)
\(-40\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\)
\(+20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{decade}\)
questions.explanation:
Break frequencies: pole at 20, zero at 400, pole at \(2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Start at DC with slope 0.
• Above \(20\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (pole): slope \(=-20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{dec}\).
• Above \(400\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (zero): slope \(=-20+20=0\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{dec}\).
• Above \(2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) (pole): slope \(=0-20=-20\ \mathrm{dB}/\mathrm{dec}\).
So between 400 and \(2000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\) the magnitude is flat (the zero cancels the first pole's slope).
Common mistake: forgetting that a zero bends the slope upward, giving −20 or −40.

questions.prompt: Preview of stability. A later skill says that a pole at \(s=p\) contributes a response term \(e^{pt}\), so a system is stable only if every pole has a negative real part. Which pole set describes a system whose natural response decays to zero?
options: Poles at \(s=-3\pm j4\)
Poles at \(s=+2\pm j5\)
Poles at \(s=0\pm j10\)
A single pole at \(s=+1\)
questions.explanation:
\(e^{pt}\) with \(p=\sigma+j\omega\) has magnitude \(e^{\sigma t}\) (the \(j\omega\) part only rotates). It decays only when \(\sigma<0\).
• \(-3\pm j4\): \(e^{-3t}\to\) decays while oscillating at \(4\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). ✔
• \(+2\pm j5\): \(e^{+2t}\) grows without bound.
• \(0\pm j10\): \(e^{0\cdot t}=1\), a sustained oscillation that neither decays nor grows (marginal).
• +1: \(e^{t}\) grows exponentially.

questions.prompt: Preview of series RLC circuits. A later skill writes the poles of the series RLC as \(s=-\omega_{0}/(2Q)\pm j\omega_{0}\sqrt{1-1/(4Q^{2})}\), where \(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}\) and \(Q=(1/R)\sqrt{L/C}\). For \(R=10\ \Omega\), \(L=1\ \mathrm{mH}\), \(C=1\ \mu\mathrm{F}\), what is the decay rate \(\alpha=-\mathrm{Re}\{s\}\) (in \(s^{-1}\)) of the circuit's natural response?
questions.explanation:
\(\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{10^{-9}}=3.162e+04\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). \(Q=(1/10)\sqrt{10^{-3}/10^{-6}}=(1/10)\sqrt{1000}=3.162\).
\(\alpha=\omega_{0}/(2Q)=3.162e+04/(2\times 3.162)=5000\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}\) (which also equals \(R/(2L)=10/(2\times 10^{-3})=5000\)).
The natural response decays as \(e^{-5000t}\) while oscillating at \(\omega_{0}\sqrt{1-1/(4Q^{2})}\approx 31{,}225\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Common mistake: using \(\omega_{0}/Q=10{,}000\) (the full bandwidth, twice \(\alpha\)).
